Apple's gaps in the upper row shrink rapidly from 19 to 16 to 7 months. Conversely, NVIDIA's data-center GPU gaps in the lower row remain near two years, at 22 and 24 months. We cannot use these announcement dates to bound a silicon program or to identify exactly when an architecture choice became too hard to change. They do not measure the pace of software change, rank release strategies, isolate any specific architecture contribution, or prove that AI tools caused a release to arrive sooner. Neither plot establishes a definitive design-cycle mismatch. Together, they illustrate why our comparisons must record the actual hardware, workload, and software exposure, rather than attempting to infer these details from public release dates.

We often use benchmarks to keep our changing workloads comparable. For example, MLPerf, an industry-standard machine learning benchmarking suite [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf], defines shared tasks and reporting rules for machine-learning systems. Within the same benchmark version, division, scenario, and accuracy target, its strict inference rules allow us to meaningfully compare results from vastly different systems [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference], all while giving submitters the freedom to optimize their software toolchains [@ReddiEtAl2021VisionBehindMLPerf]. However, this comparability is actively maintained rather than inherent to the workloads themselves. The comparison only holds true as long as our community actively maintains the tasks and run rules.[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02] Whenever those underlying rules change, we may find that an earlier comparison no longer answers the same question.

[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02]: **Metrological traceability**: A measurement result is traceable when we can relate it to a reference through a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing uncertainty [@NIST2021MetrologicalTraceability]. While our architecture benchmarks do not create this kind of formal calibration chain, we still need explicit versions for their tasks, run rules, and measurement procedures so that reviewers can verify when two results remain genuinely comparable.

For a target like Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR), the term "XR" remains far too broad to define a concrete workload, as it combines complex sensing, perception, graphics, display, interaction, latency, quality-of-experience, and energy constraints into a single concept. Throughout this book, we evaluate our system designs against five recurring workload archetypes (ResNet-50 vision, GPT-2/Llama language models, DLRM recommendation engines, MobileNetV2 mobile perception, and KWS always-on keyword spotters). Even when we employ a dedicated benchmark suite like XRBench [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench], we must still independently decide which specific traces, model versions, deadlines, input distributions, and quality targets truly matter for our design.

We must therefore treat our workload description as a precisely versioned input rather than a static name. When we document versioned traces, benchmark rules, compiler and runtime assumptions, and tool results, we allow our reviewers to independently verify whether a hardware claim still holds true. Our architecture studies also need explicit triggers that prompt us to repeat the comparison the moment one of those inputs changes. Ultimately, when our machines span an entire data center, the executable software path dictates exactly how our hardware, networks, and facility resources successfully operate as a single, unified system.

## Machine Boundary Expansion

How does expanding system boundaries to warehouse scale reshape our architectural evaluation criteria across hardware, network, and facility constraints? Warehouse scale pulls all our preceding hardware and software pressures into a single, massive architecture problem. Our server and accelerator choices no longer exist in a vacuum; they ripple outward through network topology, collective communication, cluster scheduling, failure handling, deployment policies, and even facility power and cooling. When we compare systems at this level, we must judge the delivered service and operating constraints of the entire infrastructure, rather than just admiring the efficiency of an isolated node.

Even if a single user request fits perfectly on one package, our aggregate demand, availability targets, and stringent service objectives often force us to deploy thousands of nodes. The boundary of "the computer" expands until it swallows the entire data center. As we adopt scale-out networks, sophisticated cluster software, and coherent device and memory interconnects like CXL (Compute Express Link[^fn-cxl-c02]), resource placement and sharing turn into fundamental architectural questions. We have officially entered the domain of warehouse-scale computing (WSC) [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Our architectural problem now encompasses everything from heterogeneous servers and shared cooling infrastructure to facility power limits and cluster-wide scheduling.

[^fn-cxl-c02]: **Compute Express Link (CXL)**: A cache-coherent interconnect standard for processors, accelerators, and memory devices. Its memory semantics and switching support allow us to treat device-attached or pooled memory as a system-level provisioning decision [@CXLConsortium2026CXL].

Experimenting with or simulating warehouse-scale systems is notoriously difficult, largely because component failure is a constant reality rather than an exceptional case [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. As architects, we have to piece together evidence by combining trace-driven and discrete-event models, emulation, controlled deployments, and raw production measurements. Yet, every model and measurement inevitably leaves something out. A simple trace might entirely miss the dynamic network congestion that drives crippling "tail at scale" latency [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale]. Similarly, a node that appears blazingly efficient in isolation can quickly lose that edge when bogged down by stragglers or heavy distributed coordination. Our core challenge is choosing evidence at a scale our study can actually afford, without dumbing down the system into a model that strips away the very behavior we want to review.

As we traverse these scales, we never get a clean slate, our architecture comparisons do not reset just because the system boundary expands. A single core contributes baseline policies and tricky corner cases. An accelerator brings along its own workload mapping and software interfaces. SoCs and chiplets pile on strict integration, packaging, and testing constraints. When we step up to wafer-scale and warehouse-scale systems, we inherit all those previous obligations while stacking on new burdens like repair, placement, networking, failure handling, deployment logistics, and harsh facility limits (@fig-architecture-levers).

![**A wider system boundary accumulates comparison obligations:** A credible comparison carries forward our constraints, interfaces, software paths, tool feedback, failures, and rejected alternatives established at smaller scales while adding the obligations introduced by accelerators, package composition, wafer-scale fabrics, and warehouse-scale operation.](images/F2-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-alt="Five architecture scales run from core through accelerator, system-on-chip or chiplet, wafer-scale system, and warehouse-scale system. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path, which carries constraints, interfaces, workload and software paths, tool feedback, failures, and rejected alternatives into one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

This progression is cumulative, though we aren't claiming every architectural study must simulate an entire data center. If we are comparing cores, we might legitimately stop after our microarchitecture and physical checks. But a warehouse-scale comparison can't stop there; our node's behavior only reaches the delivered service through thick layers of software, complex networks, deployment policies, and rigid facility constraints. The appropriate boundary for our study is always the smallest one that captures the effects capable of flipping our final decision. Once we pull hardware, software, network, and facility choices into a single comparison, the sheer number of possible combinations explodes far faster than our capacity to evaluate them.

## Search Space Explosion {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Why must we treat candidate design generation velocity and downstream evaluation capacity as strictly decoupled architectural resources? We must treat our capacity to produce candidate designs and our capacity to evaluate them as distinct resources. A mismatch often appears when hardware and software coupling expands the set of designs we can generate, yet our ability to check those designs fails to keep pace. We can easily conflate these two quantities simply because counting candidate production is much easier.

Even a narrow comparison can yield a staggering number of combinations. Let's look at some illustrative rather than measured arithmetic. Suppose we explore an accelerator and memory subsystem for our Lighthouse prompt across its eight stack layers. If we consider five compute organizations (vector-capable CPU, accelerator, SoC block), four ISA and ABI contract options (RV64GCV vector extensions), six memory hierarchy and data movement topologies (NoC bisection bandwidth and DRAM timing), four power envelope targets (3\ W TDP scaling), three compiler and runtime stack paths (Triton, LLVM, MLIR, domain libraries), and three physical process libraries (TSMC N7 and 3\ nm-class LP mobile process), the product is:

$$
5 \times 4 \times 6 \times 4 \times 3 \times 3
$$

We suddenly face `{python} f"{toy_design_candidates:,}"` candidate configurations before we even begin counting workload versions, process corners, thermal constraints, or reliability cases. If we check each candidate at three fidelity levels, we create `{python} f"{toy_candidate_evaluations:,}"` candidate-evaluation combinations, all before we reject a single invalid design. In our real architecture studies, these numbers grow far larger and the process takes far longer before we ever see silicon measurements.

However, this raw count tells us little about how many candidates we can actually evaluate well enough to matter. Because each surviving configuration requires an analytical model, simulator run, synthesis check, or human review, our larger choice set dramatically increases the demand for feedback. We know that cheap models reduce evaluation cost, but they cannot establish whether a choice is truly legal or whether stronger measurements will preserve its ranking. Ultimately, our practical limit is not how many configurations we can enumerate in an architecture study. Rather, it is how many we can evaluate rigorously enough to support our next design decision.

We see similar problems arise in different ways across other architecture tasks (@tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors). Mapping, design-space exploration (DSE, the systematic search over parameterized architecture families under stated constraints [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]), physical design, and software tuning do not share a single measurement scale. Instead, each task combines a massive array of possible choices with strict constraints that render only a fraction of them genuinely useful.


When we look at Timeloop [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop], an analytical framework for mapping and evaluating deep-neural-network (DNN) accelerators, we find a concrete lower bound on this combinatorial growth. For a convolutional neural network (CNN) layer with seven nested loops and a four-level memory hierarchy, our loop ordering and level-bypass choices alone produce $(7!)^4 \times (2^4)^3$ arrangements. The first factor gives us a different ordering of the seven loops at each of our four memory levels. The second factor gives us a binary bypass choice at those four levels for each of three data spaces. Our factorization choices enlarge this mapspace even further. This formula, therefore, represents neither the complete count nor a count of useful mappings. It simply isolates two sources of growth before our legality, capacity, and performance constraints step in to remove most of the candidates.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| TPU-block floorplanning | The AlphaChip paper (describing Google's reinforcement-learning layout generation engine) reported reducing placement generation from months of human effort to hours of machine time [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Routed physical quality and strong baselines still require separate evaluation. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |

: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** Mapping, accelerator DSE, floorplanning, and tensor-program tuning combine candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and different evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[25,36,28]"}

We see candidate scale emerging from entirely different parts of the system. While Timeloop and MAESTRO show us just how quickly our mapping and accelerator choices multiply, AutoTVM reminds us that our software schedule can create a massive search space even after we have locked in our hardware. Meanwhile, our floorplanning example exposes the other limit. Just because we can produce a candidate quickly does not mean we have established its routed quality.

MAESTRO makes this distinction especially clear. When we process 0.17M designs per second, we can examine its full 480M-candidate space in under an hour. In this scenario, we have access to plentiful, cheap analytical feedback. Our most difficult decision then becomes figuring out which apparent winners justify a more expensive evaluation. When we place our four anchors' candidate counts on a single logarithmic axis, we can compare them directly without making the mistake of treating equal counts as equal amounts of evaluation work (@fig-search-vs-eval-gap).

```{python}
#| label: fig-search-vs-eval-gap
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Architecture search spaces span many orders of magnitude.** The scale anchors appear on one log axis, from the toy SoC design-candidate count computed above to a lower bound on Timeloop's mapspace from loop-ordering and bypass choices [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop; @KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. Filled markers are stated or computed counts; the hollow marker is AutoTVM's order-of-magnitude estimate. Candidate count does not measure evaluation cost or evidence strength.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale strip chart plotting four search-space sizes as points: a toy SoC design space with 4,320 candidate configurations, MAESTRO's 480 million candidates, AutoTVM's roughly one billion tensor programs, and a Timeloop loop-ordering and bypass lower bound of 2.6 times ten to the eighteenth arrangements."

from math import factorial

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Data provenance (all values transcribed or computed from this chapter's text):
# - Toy SoC design candidates: 5*4*6*4*3*3 = 4,320, computed earlier in this chapter.
# - MAESTRO accelerator DSE: 480M candidates, stated [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO].
# - AutoTVM tensor programs: "on the order of billions" per GPU operator, stated
#   qualitatively (order-of-magnitude, hollow marker) [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM].
# - Timeloop loop-ordering and bypass lower bound: (7!)^4 * (2^4)^3 ~= 2.6e18,
#   computed from the stated expression [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. Values not
#   recomputed from sources.
# As-of: 2026-07-14.

toy_candidates = 5 * 4 * 6 * 4 * 3 * 3
timeloop_mapspace = factorial(7) ** 4 * (2**4) ** 3

rows = [
    {"label": "Toy SoC design candidates", "note": "computed in this chapter", "value": toy_candidates, "right": "$4.3\\times10^{3}$", "stated": True},
    {"label": "MAESTRO accelerator DSE", "note": "480M candidates, stated", "value": 4.8e8, "right": "$4.8\\times10^{8}$", "stated": True},
    {"label": "AutoTVM tensor programs", "note": "order of billions, approximate", "value": 1e9, "right": "$\\sim\\!10^{9}$", "stated": False},
    {"label": "Timeloop ordering + bypass lower bound", "note": "$(7!)^{4}\\times(2^{4})^{3}$, computed", "value": timeloop_mapspace, "right": "$2.6\\times10^{18}$", "stated": True},
]

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.95, 2.75))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.42, right=0.82, top=0.79, bottom=0.22)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(2e1, 4e19),
    xticks=[1e2, 1e5, 1e8, 1e11, 1e14, 1e17],
    xticklabels=["$10^{2}$", "$10^{5}$", "$10^{8}$", "$10^{11}$", "$10^{14}$", "$10^{17}$"],
    xlabel="search-space size (candidate configurations)",
)

for y, row in enumerate(rows):
    ax.axhline(y, color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.65, zorder=0)
    if row["stated"]:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["designspace"], edgecolor=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-0.86, y - 0.17, row["label"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(-0.86, y + 0.23, row["note"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(1.04, y, row["right"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.1, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["designspace_ink"], clip_on=False)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

Notice how our toy count sits in the thousands, MAESTRO and AutoTVM cluster near $10^9$, and Timeloop's computed lower bound lies almost ten orders of magnitude farther to the right. We use AutoTVM's hollow marker to distinguish its order-of-magnitude estimate from the explicitly stated or computed counts. While this full span covers nearly fifteen orders of magnitude, the horizontal position only encodes our candidate count. It tells us absolutely nothing about the cost, fidelity, or decision strength of a single evaluation. As architects, we must decide which choices are truly worth testing and exactly how many reliable evaluations our architecture study can afford.

We must always remember that our search capacity and evaluation capacity draw from completely separate budgets. ArchGym, an open-source machine learning gym for architecture design space exploration [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], clearly shows us why our exploration methods require fair, reproducible comparisons under common environments and shared sample budgets. Throughout this book, we apply an even broader accounting rule. We compare evaluation fidelity, tool cost, total compute, and engineering effort, rather than simply equalizing candidate counts alone. Although a fast estimator can drastically increase the number of candidates receiving a quick score, it does not increase the number of candidates receiving a check strong enough to support our final commitment.

While an executable software path is absolutely necessary, it still fails to establish how many candidates we can check strongly enough to support a robust decision. Our next real limit is the actual capacity and fidelity of our evaluation and verification.

## Physical Limits and Throughput

How do physical constraints and simulation throughput bounds govern the maximum resolution of our architectural comparisons? We can keep growing our design space, but physics, budgets, and schedules still bound our comparisons. Physics dictates what we can actually build, power, and cool, while fixed program budgets and schedules dictate how much we can check before we commit to a tapeout. Though more resources might expand our evaluation capacity, they never remove underlying physical limits nor make our available time and money unbounded.

### Physical Constraints {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

When we compare architectures, physical effects introduce two distinct problems. First, our early models might omit an effect that later overturns our initial rankings. Second, the definitive measurements that would settle the question often cost too much to run on every candidate. Consequently, a design that looks sound at our architectural abstraction can still fail due to a thermal hotspot or severe IR drop, revealing that our comparison masked a consequential physical effect. Furthermore, reliability narrows our viable space even further. Phenomena like soft errors, process variation [@Borkar2005ReliableSystems], and silicon aging, including Negative Bias Temperature Instability (NBTI) and Hot Carrier Injection (HCI), directly affect viability in demanding domains like automotive systems governed by ISO 26262 [@ISO2018Iso26262]. To build confidence, we must often look to evidence from fault injection, aging simulation, physical and circuit analysis, accelerated testing, and production data.

Consider data movement, for example, which can easily reverse an early ranking based purely on compute. As we move data through a memory hierarchy, we often consume far more energy than we do performing arithmetic operations. Horowitz's widely used estimates help quantify this stark difference [@Horowitz2014Energy]. If we rely on a compute-only comparison, we risk ranking the wrong design first. Ultimately, our results depend heavily on where the data resides, how often it moves, who schedules it, what locality we can exploit, which precision we find acceptable, and what our software stack can express.

When we plot the gap between arithmetic and memory-access energy on a logarithmic scale, it spans roughly four orders of magnitude (@fig-data-movement-energy-scale). In the cited 45\ nm data, a 32-bit integer addition costs a fraction of a picojoule. However, an 8 KB SRAM access costs about two orders of magnitude more, and accessing off-chip dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) costs roughly four orders of magnitude more. We should treat these values as order-of-magnitude anchors rather than exact predictions for a current process node.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Rough Horowitz 45\ nm energy values show why architecture comparisons must represent locality, buffering, precision, scheduling, and memory hierarchy rather than counting arithmetic alone [@Horowitz2014Energy]. The values are transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors, including the source's 1.3--2.6\ nJ DRAM range, not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, SRAM accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, add_note_box, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv

rows = [
    {"display_label": "32b integer add", "display_note": "baseline arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 0.1, "energy_high_pj": 0.1, "right_label": "1$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "32b floating-point add", "display_note": "local arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 0.9, "energy_high_pj": 0.9, "right_label": "9$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "32b integer multiply", "display_note": "local arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 3.0, "energy_high_pj": 3.0, "right_label": "30$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "32b floating-point multiply", "display_note": "local arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 4.0, "energy_high_pj": 4.0, "right_label": "40$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "8 KB SRAM access", "display_note": "64b cache access", "energy_low_pj": 10, "energy_high_pj": 10, "right_label": "100$\\times$", "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"display_label": "32 KB SRAM access", "display_note": "64b cache access", "energy_low_pj": 20, "energy_high_pj": 20, "right_label": "200$\\times$", "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"display_label": "1 MB SRAM access", "display_note": "on-chip memory access", "energy_low_pj": 100, "energy_high_pj": 100, "right_label": "1000$\\times$", "color": COLORS["orange"]},
    {"display_label": "off-chip DRAM access", "display_note": "off-chip memory access", "energy_low_pj": 1300, "energy_high_pj": 2600, "right_label": "13k--26k$\\times$", "color": COLORS["red"]},
]

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.45))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.17)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)
add_note_box(fig, "Rough 45 nm values from Horowitz; use for orders of magnitude.", xywh=(0.14, 0.035, 0.72, 0.075), fontsize=5.5)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

As we look at the chart, the rows progress from arithmetic operations through on-chip SRAM to off-chip DRAM at the far right. We show the DRAM marker as a range rather than a single point, and we anchor the ratios on the right relative to the 32-bit integer addition. While advanced nodes certainly change these exact values, our comparison still supports an order-of-magnitude locality argument rather than acting as a current-node energy estimate. It reminds us that we absolutely must model our memory hierarchy before we rank candidates.

To frame our thinking, we often use a helpful architecture-level decomposition:
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} =
E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} +
E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} +
E_{\mathrm{leakage}} .
$$
We intend this as a structural breakdown, not a rigorous circuit-level energy model, and it delivers a clear lesson in diminishing returns. This decomposition directly reflects two persistent physical limits. First, Wulf and McKee's Memory Wall [@WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall] highlights that logic performance scaling continuously outpaces DRAM access latency improvements, elevating off-chip memory access into the primary latency and energy bottleneck. Second, as multi-core and accelerator tile counts scale, Network-on-Chip (NoC) bisection bandwidth contention becomes a governing throughput bottleneck. High inter-tile communication and memory traffic saturate physical wiring and router buffers across die bisection cuts, causing routing congestion and severe backpressure. If an optimization focuses solely on compute efficiency while ignoring memory hierarchy and interconnect topology, unoptimized data movement and leakage terms quickly dominate system energy and render the design physically infeasible (@fig-waterbed-effect).

![**Lower compute energy can hide a worse system total.** The illustrative candidate reduces compute energy but increases memory and interconnect energy enough to exceed our baseline total. A comparison that omits data movement can therefore rank the worse of the two designs first. The bar heights show the relationship and are not measured energy breakdowns.](images/F2-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="85%" fig-alt="Bar chart comparing a baseline energy breakdown with an illustrative candidate whose lower compute energy is outweighed by higher memory and interconnect energy."}

Notice how our baseline and candidate in the figure differ in more than just arithmetic. While our candidate successfully lowers the compute term, its added memory traffic and communication penalties inflate the system total well beyond the baseline. Although we use illustrative numbers here, the resulting reversal is exactly our point. An early proxy might strongly favor a design that ultimately loses once we properly account for the costs of moving data through the system. We explore this specific proxy-mismatch failure directly in @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

We must give interconnect costs the same rigorous attention as memory movement. Our on-chip networks, package links, memory interfaces, collective operations, and host-device protocols strictly limit what our designs can sustain. During early logical synthesis and architectural modeling, we rely on approximate interconnect estimates, whereas detailed placement and routing expose our actual topology, congestion, and parasitic delays [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. Because of this gap, a highly parallel accelerator might score exceptionally well in our early models, only to fail timing or routing during physical implementation. The fundamental failure here isn't that our early tools completely ignore wires; rather, it is that a clever optimizer will always exploit whatever our inexpensive models leave out.

::: {.callout-historical-perspective title="Seymour Cray and the Physical Wire-Length Limit"}
**The breakthrough.** When Seymour Cray designed the CRAY-1 supercomputer in 1975, achieving a 80\ MHz clock frequency required ensuring that no backplane module interconnect wire exceeded 8 inches in length, limiting signal propagation delay strictly to 1 nanosecond [@Russell1978Cray1].

**The lineage.** To achieve this physical constraint, Cray arranged the mainframe chassis in a 270-degree "C" shape, placing modules on the inner radius to minimize physical distance while integrating Freon-cooled copper bars directly into the frame to manage extreme thermal density.

**The synthesis lesson.** Cray's physical geometry demonstrates that high-level computer architecture cannot be decoupled from physical packaging, signal propagation speeds, and thermal dissipation. In AI-driven design space search, an optimizer that ranks candidates without incorporating physical interconnect and thermal bounds will inevitably generate microarchitectures that cannot be routed or cooled in real silicon.
:::


Because timing, placement, routing, IR drop, thermal behavior, power delivery, leakage, signoff, and test requirements can easily overturn an architectural choice, we must consider relevant electronic design automation (EDA) and physical-design constraints as early as possible. These deep physical checks rely heavily on stateful tools, meaning a repeated run becomes entirely invalid if stale constraints or cached netlists survive from a previous candidate. While @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces covers our detailed tool isolation and execution mechanics, our core point here is that a clean tool state remains an absolute prerequisite for a valid comparison. For example, local power and thermal density can flag a dense accelerator mapping as highly risky long before implementation, even if its average power comfortably clears an early limit.

Once we have a placed netlist and a current profile, later IR-drop analysis [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet] and thermal signoff can either confirm or clear that risk. We should also remember that Thermal Design Power (TDP), which serves as a target for sizing our cooling solution rather than a strict measure of sustained power draw, is not our only limit [@Intel2014QuarkThermalGuide]. For instance, rapid clock-gating transitions or 512-bit SIMD vector lane wakeups induce severe step-current transients ($di/dt$), causing localized $L \cdot \frac{di}{dt}$ voltage droops on the power grid that force conservative frequency guardbanding or dedicated Emergency Voltage Mitigation (EVM) circuits. If we employ early physical estimates, workload-aware power models, and closer coordination between our microarchitecture and physical design, we can expose these subtle risks long before final signoff.

**Measure active-frequency policy.** When we add 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores, we raise our peak floating-point throughput. However, sustained wide-vector execution might raise power and power-delivery demand enough to force the processor to reduce its operating frequency. Peak vector width alone does not determine our final application speed; as architects, we must carefully measure the active-frequency policy alongside our exact mix of vector and nonvector work on the target processor.

During timing signoff, we evaluate multiple analysis views that pair operating modes with specific process corners using static timing signoff tools like Cadence Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus]. We often find that our design might clear one view but completely fail another. Because our physical-design tools rely on heuristic optimization, a single failed closure attempt rarely tells us whether our candidate or a flawed tool setup caused the failure. When we carefully compare constraints, seeds, and repeated outcomes, we can better separate true design flaws from tool artifacts.


Design Rule Checks (DRC) introduce yet another rigorous physical constraint. Our routing must satisfy restricted design rules, including stringent minimum wire and via spacing [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. Simply moving a single macro can spawn numerous violations, and repairing just one can alter neighboring routes and expose fresh errors. If our automated flow cannot interpret these markers intelligently, we inevitably dump a massive, repetitive cleanup and rerouting burden onto our implementation team.

Furthermore, artifact-producing flows introduce a frustrating traceability problem for each of these physical constraints. If our high-level tool emits RTL and a physical-design tool reports a thermal failure much later, tracing that failure back to the specific architectural decision that caused it becomes incredibly difficult. Since we can often rerun a saved RTL or topology artifact for deeper inspection, our design team must diligently preserve the emitted artifacts, parameters, and tool states rather than hoping we can somehow recreate them later. When we evaluate these physical constraints, we also face the challenge of bridging the deep semantic gap between our high-level proposals and intricate EDA formats like LEF/DEF and Liberty timing files.[^fn-lef-def-c02]

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: In our place-and-route flows, LEF carries the abstract physical information we use to place and connect blocks, while DEF captures the fully placed and routed state of our specific design [@Si2LEFDEF]. Meanwhile, Liberty provides characterized cell models covering timing, power, noise, and related behaviors [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat]. We rely on these implementation formats to expose the crucial details missing from our high-level architectural descriptions.

To manage this complexity, we increasingly turn to multifidelity methods that pair abundant, inexpensive estimates with carefully selected high-fidelity evaluations. We retain the stronger model to repeatedly check the accuracy of our proxy, a broad strategy familiar across all of engineering optimization, not just architecture [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Our physical constraints demand exactly this level of care. If we know our early model omits timing, congestion, thermal behavior, or data movement, we must secure a more robust model before we confidently compare more candidates.

While an inexpensive energy proxy can absolutely support our early screening efforts, our finalists require an accurate, current power model before we can make binding power or efficiency decisions. We encounter this same limitation when measuring whatever metric we happen to be optimizing. A design can easily lead on the figures advertised in a standard data sheet, yet still fall woefully behind on the actual work a real program executes.

The evolution of AMD's Bulldozer architecture, its later FX-9590 product, and the subsequent Zen transition perfectly illustrates this dangerous gap between easy-to-count specifications and real-world workload behavior [@BurgessEtAl2011Bulldozer; @AMDFXQuickReference; @AMDZen].

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** In their Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011), AMD chose to group two integer cores behind a shared front-end and floating-point unit while aggressively pursuing high clock frequencies. Since core counts and frequencies were easy to advertise, they made compelling marketing points. When we share structures, the architects explicitly traded some per-thread capacity to maximize overall throughput.

**The gap.** Unfortunately, those impressive figures did not reflect how real workloads actually used the machine. The shared structures quickly became severe bottlenecks whenever two threads competed for them, and aggressively raising the clocks dramatically increased power consumption. In fact, AMD's later FX-9590 quick-reference specification had to list a staggering 220\ W power rating.

**The lesson.** We must always rank our candidates on the metrics their true workloads reward, rather than the numbers that are easiest to count. In silicon, discovering that gap is painfully expensive, because it only becomes undeniable after we ship the design. AMD eventually addressed this by introducing the Zen microarchitecture, returning to a renewed, disciplined emphasis on core performance and efficiency.
:::

Because physical constraints and reliability concerns define a massive search space, no early model will ever eliminate our need for the robust physical tools required to validate our final claims. As architects, we must intuitively understand exactly which lower-cost estimates are safe for broad screening, and which rigorous checks retain the power to overturn our rankings.

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

As we design larger systems, we expose vastly more candidate configurations, software states, physical corners, and failure modes. Expanding our choice space inherently drives up our demand for simulator runs, synthesis runs, physical-design tools, verification passes, and expert review. We simply cannot run every candidate through every available tool. Since these evaluations consume varying mixtures of compute clusters, software licenses, project schedule, and human attention, our feedback loop starves whenever an architectural study demands more checking capacity than our available people and tools can possibly provide.

Our evaluation tools form a broad spectrum where adjacent tiers often sit orders of magnitude apart in throughput, cost, and setup time. Suppose we have a simulator like `gem5` that sustains ten to one hundred thousand instructions per second. At those agonizing rates, simulating just one real-time second of a workload retiring one billion instructions per second takes roughly three to twenty-eight hours. Fast parallel simulators like `Sniper` or compiled C++ RTL models generated via `Verilator` run significantly faster, while hardware emulation platforms (such as `Cadence Palladium`, an enterprise hardware emulation system, or `Synopsys ZeBu`, a high-throughput emulation engine) and FPGA prototypes (like `FireSim`, an FPGA-accelerated full-system simulation platform [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]) accelerate execution even further. Yet, each step up the fidelity spectrum demands different hardware, complex logic synthesis (via open-source engines like `Yosys` or industrial suites), and substantial bring-up costs. Since actual rates always depend on the model, workload, host, tool, and platform, our fundamental budgeting question isn't just whether a candidate *can* be measured, but rather which candidates have actually earned the right to consume an expensive evaluation tier.

To cope, we have long rationed our expensive evaluations through clever abstraction and statistical sampling. For example, SimPoint, a profile-driven simulation sampling framework [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], helps us isolate highly representative program regions, while SMARTS, a statistically rigorous sampling methodology [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS], gives us rigorous error bounds for sampled simulation. We employ analytical models, reduced workloads, and multifidelity evaluation to serve this exact same purpose across different design levels. Because every one of these techniques trades some fidelity for capacity, we must clearly state what our cheaper evaluations preserve and explicitly flag which candidates still mandate a stronger check.

Making this allocation decision is incredibly difficult. While generating or scoring one more candidate might feel cheap, an inaccurate screening tool can tragically discard a breakthrough design or blindly advance a fundamentally weak one into our most expensive stages. We have to decide which inexpensive checks can safely reject a candidate, which nagging uncertainties demand stronger tools, and which measurements are most likely to completely flip our final decision. If we fail to make these distinctions, generating candidates faster merely dumps more hopeless work into our design program's most expensive, back-end stages.

The staggering costs of leading-edge chip development perfectly illustrate the scale of this constraint. Although public estimates vary and shouldn't be taken as universal accounting rules, they paint a clear picture. The Semiconductor Industry Association reports that designing a latest-node chip skyrocketed from about \$30M for a 65\ nm node in 2006 to over \$540M for a 5\ nm node in 2020, representing a massive $18\times$ increase [@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign]. A McKinsey analysis confirms this order of magnitude, estimating roughly \$175M for a 10\ nm design, \$300M for 7\ nm, and \$540M for 5\ nm once we include validation, IP qualification, and related development costs [@BauerEtAl2020SemiconductorDesignManufacturing]. We must recognize that these estimates cover far more than just masks or wafers; they capture the immense architecture, design, validation, verification, IP, tooling, and human engineering labor required to succeed.

If we force a respin, we add massive fabrication, validation, and schedule penalties before we even learn whether our correction actually worked. Ultimately, our heavy investments in simulation, emulation, and rigorous signoff exist precisely to minimize the terrifying probability of ever paying for that iteration again.

### Verification Bottlenecks

We all know that verification faces a terrifying exponential state-space upper bound, even though smart structuring, clever abstractions, and advanced verification methods ultimately govern how much work we actually perform. Adding just a single state-holding bit doubles our number of encoded states, meaning a design with $n$ such bits can technically encode up to $2^n$ states. Thankfully, the reachable subset is usually far smaller because it depends tightly on our reset and next-state logic; this is precisely why our verification jobs don't just blindly enumerate every encoded state.

However, that theoretical upper bound absolutely rules out verifying every relevant property through brute-force enumeration. Instead, we must artfully combine coverage goals, SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), formal proofs, constrained-random testing with production simulators like `Synopsys VCS` (an industrial SystemVerilog logic simulator), fast compiled C++ simulation using `Verilator`, deep regressions, unresolved-defect reviews, and hard-earned engineering judgment. We view a flattening bug-discovery curve as just one key input to our tapeout decision, rather than a standalone, infallible rule. Crucially, a sudden flood of novel architectural candidates forces our team to repeat substantial portions of this incredibly exhausting work.

For these reasons, our architectural evaluations must explicitly weigh verification effort alongside the classic pillars of Power, Performance, and Area (PPA). For instance, a highly speculative cache-coherence protocol might demonstrate a superb measured performance gain, yet it remains a terrible choice if we cannot thoroughly check its complex new states and interactions within our given design-program budget.

We rely on formal verification and simulation to attack entirely different parts of this problem. When we simulate using engines like VCS or Verilator, we exercise selected behaviors under highly specific stimuli. When we use formal methods (supported by tools like Yosys for formal checking), we mathematically prove a stated property across all possible behaviors covered by our model and its baseline assumptions, though our formal capacity drops sharply depending on the property, abstraction level, and sequential state. To manage this, we often use bounded model checking (BMC) to search behavior only up to a chosen cycle depth. We also lean heavily on combinational equivalence checking, which elegantly skirts the sequential state explosion by merely proving that two combinational descriptions implement the exact same Boolean function. Despite these tools, intricate sequential protocols, liveness guarantees, and broad system interactions will always require us to deploy a carefully balanced mix of formal checking and robust simulation [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

Our industry has grappled publicly with this intense verification pressure for over a quarter of a century. As far back as 2001, the ITRS Design chapter famously declared verification "a bottleneck that has now reached crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design]. Today, the Semiconductor Research Corporation's MAPT roadmap still explicitly warns of a widening verification gap looming across our future transitions [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. While this rich history makes verification an indispensable constraint to check whenever someone proposes generating architectural candidates faster, it doesn't automatically imply that verification will be the absolute limiting constraint in every single design program.

Yet the math is inescapable. If we can produce new register-transfer level (RTL) candidates faster than we can create the properties, tests, coverage metrics, and human reviews required to bless them, our rapid generation speed does absolutely nothing to improve our final tapeout decision. This harsh reality powerfully grounds the abstract state-space argument directly into the grinding daily work of a hardware team.

Looking at the workforce, Foster's summary of the 2022 Wilson Research Group functional-verification study confirms that demand for integrated circuit (IC) and ASIC verification engineers exploded nearly three times faster than demand for design engineers between 2007 and 2022, roughly 146 percent versus 50 percent (@fig-verification-demand-scissors). Furthermore, mean peak staffing hovered around one verification engineer for every design engineer across most market segments. In complex processor projects, that ratio surged as high as five to one, and astonishingly, even design engineers reported spending 49 percent of their time entirely on verification tasks in 2022 [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy].

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak demand for IC/ASIC verification engineers grew about 146 percent from 2007 to 2022 while demand for design engineers grew about 50 percent, a 6.2 versus 2.7 percent compound annual growth rate [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers have printed data labels in the published study figures; hollow 2022 markers are chart-read approximations constrained by the study's stated growth figures.
#| out-width: "78%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-line chart indexing engineer demand to 2007, with verification-engineer demand rising to about 2.5 times its 2007 level by 2022 while design-engineer demand reaches about 1.5 times, opening a widening gap between the lines."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA

# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries). 2007-2020

# values have printed data labels; 2022 values are chart-read, constrained by

# the study's stated callouts of +50% design and +146% verification demand

# growth since 2007 (2.7% vs 6.2% CAGR).

# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv

years = [2007, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2022]
design = [7.8, 8.5, 10.5, 10.3, 11.7]
verif = [4.8, 8.4, 11.6, 11.4, 11.8]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(years[:-1], verif_idx[:-1], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
ax.scatter(years[:-1], design_idx[:-1], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)

# 2022 values are chart-read approximations: draw them hollow

ax.scatter([years[-1]], [verif_idx[-1]], s=26, facecolors="white",
           edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([years[-1]], [design_idx[-1]], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white",
           edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(2022.6, verif_idx[-1], "verification\nengineers (+146%)", va="center",
        fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)
ax.text(2022.6, design_idx[-1], "design\nengineers (+50%)", va="center",
        fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(2006, 2023)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks([2007, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2022])
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel("mean peak demand vs. 2007", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```
