
Because we indexed the two lines in @fig-verification-demand-scissors to their 2007 values, they highlight relative growth rather than absolute staffing levels, and the verification line clearly rises much faster. We display filled markers through 2020 to represent printed data labels from the published figures, while our hollow 2022 endpoints serve as chart-read approximations constrained tightly by the published growth rates. Naturally, these staffing trends don't pinpoint a single universal cause for the disparity, nor do they perfectly diagnose the bottleneck in any single project. However, they unequivocally prove that checking our designs steadily consumes an ever-growing share of our engineering capacity across the surveyed projects. Once a generated candidate reaches this late stage, it is decidedly no longer free to evaluate. Hardware is notoriously unforgiving; a defect in shipped silicon is incredibly costly to address and we can rarely undo it cleanly. The infamous 1994 Pentium FDIV flaw perfectly illustrates why our early checks matter so much, as a bug stemming from just five omitted lookup table entries [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision] forced Intel to report a staggering \$475M pretax charge for replacements and related costs [@Intel1995PentiumCharge]. More recently, the devastating Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre] fully exposed dangerous microarchitectural side channels hiding deep in our speculative execution engines. Although published evaluations demonstrate varying workload- and processor-dependent performance hits when we deploy transient-execution defenses [@CanellaEtAl2019Transient], those software defenses cannot erase the underlying hardware mechanism. Together, these painful episodes prove how quickly a hardware flaw transforms into an expensive, long-lived liability once we ship a design, a burden that replacement programs, customer support, or software workarounds can only mitigate, never cleanly remove.

While that Pentium charge highlights the fallout from a single escaped defect, our leading-edge development inherently raises the cost of our commitment even when we avoid a public recall entirely. Arm's 2023 prospectus shares International Business Strategies (IBS) estimates of \$249M to design a 7\ nm chip and an astonishing \$725M for a 2\ nm chip [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. We must read these figures as broad estimates rather than rigid, universal project prices. Even so, they powerfully illustrate that high-fidelity evaluation and physical implementation at the leading edge eagerly consume our massive engineering budgets, not just our simulator cycles.

For us as architects, the internal composition of that 2\ nm estimate matters far more than its frightening total. Remarkably, software development, verification, and IP qualification together swallow up 71 percent of the total 2\ nm budget in the published IBS prospectus breakdown [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The durable takeaway is unavoidable. The vast majority of our estimated budget pays for the software and checking work required to make a chip genuinely usable and trustworthy, rather than merely paying to generate the raw RTL design artifact.

This harsh reality actually predates the advanced nodes that produced these numbers. The 2001 ITRS Design chapter observed that software already accounted for 80 percent of embedded-systems development costs [@ITRS2001Design]. We treat this as another historical testament to the sheer scale of software and verification costs, which remain the dominant cost drivers across process node transitions.

Ultimately, these staggering costs fundamentally alter what we should consider a true architectural improvement. Simply producing more architectural candidates offers us no real value if every surviving design dumps massive simulation, synthesis, physical-design, verification, and code-review workloads onto an already overflowing queue. To succeed, our team must cleanly distill an ocean of scattered tool results into a crisp, undeniable comparison that our expert reviewers can actually inspect, and that our leadership can confidently use to make the final tapeout decision.

## Compounding Loop Pressures {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

How do cross-layer design pressures compound to create critical evaluation bottlenecks across the architecture loop? These pressures interact rather than merely accumulate. As we specialize our designs, we expand the choice set; each hardware choice creates new software obligations. Our software changes can easily make the original workload description stale, while physical effects might reverse whatever rankings remain. Every candidate that survives this gauntlet then heaps more work onto our plates, demanding simulation, implementation tools, verification, and expert review.

This tight coupling matters because optimizing one stage often just pushes the bottleneck somewhere else. If we generate candidates faster, we might simply flood our evaluation queue. Speed up simulation, and we risk churning out more results than our reviewers can meaningfully reconcile. Sometimes, building a more accurate physical model only reveals that none of our available choices can hit the target. Ultimately, the size of our design space, our evaluation capacity, and the quality of our decisions are entirely different quantities, cranking up the first does not guarantee any improvement in the other two.

Rather than hunting for a single, universal bottleneck, our teams should look for the specific work that currently throttles progress. We can look at the age and size of our simulation or verification queues, track the fraction of candidates rejected as illegal, or count the repeated tool runs and changing inputs. We might also watch where our results stall out waiting for expert judgment. While broad industry trends provide context, we need these local, concrete measures to diagnose the actual constraints of our own design programs.

We define the *Rejection-Bound Scissors Gap* as the widening divergence between candidate generation velocity and evaluation capacity, where automated methods produce proposed designs faster than downstream verification tools and human architects can execute rejection checks to accept or disqualify them (@fig-scissors-gap). Any candidate caught in that gap has been generated but has not been evaluated deeply enough to support a defensible decision. It is dangerously easy for teams to let this gap grow unnoticed, since raw candidate counts fail to distinguish a design that actually survived rigorous review from one that has not even reached an evaluator.

Missing or stale information only makes this worse, creating a vicious, reinforcing bottleneck. Bad data admits invalid choices, squanders our scarce evaluation cycles on them, and ultimately overloads our review process with the resulting conflicts. As review gets delayed, we are left trying to make our next decisions with even less current information (@fig-bottleneck-causal-loop). We cannot break this cycle just by generating candidates or running evaluations faster; we have to repair the underlying information and decision boundaries.

![**A local bottleneck can reinforce itself.** Missing information admits invalid choices, which waste our scarce evaluation and overload our review; delayed review then worsens the information available for the next choice.](images/F2-bottleneck-causal-loop){#fig-bottleneck-causal-loop width="72%" fig-alt="Four-node reinforcing cycle connecting missing information, invalid choices, wasted evaluation, and overloaded review."}

Left unchecked, this local cycle can easily balloon into a massive capacity gap across the entire design program. While the causal loop traces exactly how we create this unresolved work, the "scissors" model illustrates what happens when that work piles up faster than our tools and reviewers can ever process it (@fig-scissors-gap).

![**Design work can outpace our capacity to examine it.** In this conceptual relationship, the two straight lines cross as our design scope and result volume increase. The widening region beyond the crossing holds candidates that we have generated but never evaluated well enough to accept or reject.](images/F2-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="85%" fig-alt="Conceptual diverging-line diagram in which tool and reviewer capacity initially exceeds work awaiting evaluation. The straight lines cross as design scope and result volume increase, after which work awaiting evaluation rises faster and creates widening unsettled work."}

Looking at the left side of the figure, our tool and reviewer capacity can initially absorb the work arriving for evaluation. However, the red line crosses the blue line the moment that pending evaluation and review work outstrips our available capacity. The shaded region beyond that crossover represents unresolved work rather than a measured backlog, and the horizontal axis tracks our increasing design scope and result volume rather than elapsed time. While these straight lines are purely schematic, they do not assert a strict measured rate or functional relationship, our own search-space examples show just how quickly a design study can flood us with candidates. Meanwhile, verification-staffing data provides a sobering, measured example of the sheer engineering effort required to check increasingly complex designs. Together, these factors make a mismatch between candidate arrivals and our completion capacity highly plausible, but we can only establish the truth of it for our own design programs through careful, local observation.

The scissors in @fig-scissors-gap has a well-established ancestor in our discipline. Back in 2001, the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors highlighted a design productivity gap, warning that available transistors were growing much faster than our ability to meaningfully design them [@ITRS2001Design]. We responded to that gap largely by raising the level of abstraction, embracing RTL synthesis and IP reuse so that a single engineer's decision could govern many more transistors. Two decades later, the Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) and Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) echoed this exact shortfall in their Decadal Plan for Semiconductors. They identified a persistent design gap between what the technology permits and what we can realistically build in a reasonable time, calling for a tenfold or greater leap in design productivity (though they scoped this target to analog and mixed-signal work rather than the entire design loop) [@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. That history sets the bar for what we will explore in this book. For AI assistance to truly earn its place, we must be able to show exactly how it changes our workload without weakening the critical checks we need to make confident decisions.

While a growing evaluation or review queue makes one type of mismatch painfully visible, not every constraint manifests as a neat queue. An architecture study might simply be missing a workload trace, a packaging constraint, or a software model that would otherwise completely reverse our findings. We might find that our available choices exclude the specific interface or memory organization we need to hit our targets. Sometimes the decisive tool is just too expensive to run broadly, or our results are fully baked but still sitting idle, waiting for expert judgment. Ultimately, the most useful question is not what category label we slap on our whole effort. The real question is what specific work is currently blocking our next architectural decision, and which checks must remain absolutely authoritative if we decide to accelerate that work.

This nuance explains why the widening region in @fig-scissors-gap is conditional rather than universal. We might find our design programs limited by candidate production, while others are choked by evaluation, verification, missing information, or even a fundamentally infeasible design space. The figure only transforms into a local diagnosis when our own programmatic measurements prove that the work awaiting our evaluation or review is genuinely growing faster than we can complete it.

## Targeting AI Assistance {#sec-feedback-and-verification-become-the-bottleneck}

Where can AI assistance effectively relieve design bottlenecks without displacing authoritative physical and software verification checks? When we consider applying AI to our design process, we first need to identify the specific bottlenecks holding back our decisions. If our design context is stale, we need tools that can reconcile conflicting information; if strong evaluations are too costly, we need predictive screening before invoking expensive simulators. Sometimes, we lack an executable artifact altogether and need automated construction, or our choice space simply exceeds our evaluation budget and requires guided search. Even mundane tasks like repeated tool operation and triage place enormous pressure on our attention. To choose the right assistance, we must ask which specific limit is slowing progress in our current architecture study.

We can look to existing research for concrete examples of how these bottlenecks are being addressed. When we adapt models to our internal design collateral, we can quickly retrieve and organize critical information, while tool-using systems can directly translate our requests into electronic design automation (EDA) commands (using domain-adapted LLMs like ChipNeMo for design queries or ChatEDA for flow automation [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]). If simulation time is our limit, predictive models and learned physical estimators (such as PowerNet, a deep-learning model for fast voltage-drop estimation [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet]) can screen out poor candidates long before we run detailed analyses [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling]. Similarly, when exploring complex accelerators, we can use learned search heuristics to guide our exploration [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo]. If verification-authoring effort is what holds us back, we can deploy generators (such as AutoBench, an LLM-driven testbench generation framework [@QiuEtAl2024AutoBench]) to draft our testbenches. Scaling up to the warehouse level, we see how learned schedulers (such as DeepRM, a reinforcement-learning resource manager [@MaoEtAl2016DeepRM]) and reconfigurable fabrics allow us to evaluate automated decisions against cluster-level workloads and stringent system-level constraints [@JouppiEtAl2023TPUv4].

Software co-evolution presents another compelling target for assistance. We can deploy tool-using regression systems to ingest new compiler builds, rerun our architecture benchmarks, and notify us whenever a candidate's standing shifts. While such a system dramatically reduces our manual reevaluation workload, it ultimately cannot decide if that software change invalidates our core architecture comparison. As architects, we still have to use our judgment to determine whether those software updates could actually reverse our design decisions.

While regression automation is one specific application of AI on the software side, Amarasinghe's Compiler 2.0 proposal points us toward a much broader opportunity. The argument is that modern multicore processors, vector instructions, accelerators, and heterogeneous systems have fundamentally pushed the performance burden back onto software developers. When we modernize our compilers through better abstractions, machine learning, and other advanced techniques, we can begin to lift that burden [@Amarasinghe2026Compiler20CSAIL]. However, even this level of assistance still must produce a functional, executable path and explicitly demonstrate its benefit on the specific hardware and workloads we are reviewing.

Of course, every form of assistance incurs a distinct cost and introduces new ways our systems can fail. To clarify these trade-offs, the comparison in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound connects each bottleneck to the specific engineering work we might reduce, as well as the independent checks we must retain. Ultimately, we only find a method useful when the reduction in manual effort is truly worth the additional data, compute, tool calls, and rigorous review it demands of us.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing details or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and our architectural judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change our decisions. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and our first pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, authoritative tool verdicts, and expert review where required. |

: **Each use retains an independent check.** While AI may reduce our manual work in information search, evaluation, artifact creation, design-space exploration, or tool-operation, it never replaces the provenance, calibration, engineering tools, or architectural judgment that establishes our final result. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[20,29,23,28]"}

We often deploy several forms of assistance to address different bottlenecks within the same design program. However, combining them does not magically make our results self-validating. If every component in our pipeline depends on the same incomplete workload description or flawed model, our complete system might look internally consistent while being completely wrong.

Any useful comparison must therefore fully account for the cost of assistance itself. We have to supply surrogate models with data from stronger tools. Our generative tools often add numerous new candidates to a full evaluation queue, and our tool-using systems readily consume software licenses, simulation time, and our own review attention. Ultimately, our limiting work and our required independent checks determine whether a particular use of assistance actually helps us. Once we identify those factors, our next question is which method or combination best fits the work, a topic we develop further in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization.

Importantly, our evaluation test must also allow us to reject AI assistance entirely. AI is simply the wrong intervention when we already have an established deterministic method that solves the limiting task within our required cost and time budgets. We should also reject it when a proposed learned method lacks representative training data, or when we cannot construct an independent check commensurate with the consequences of failure. It is an equally poor trade when inference time, tool calls, and added human review cost us more than the engineering work they supposedly save. Sometimes, our real obstacle is an infeasible system requirement or a complex decision that no amount of faster search can settle. In those cases, the right answer is sticking to a conventional method, fundamentally changing our architecture problem, or simply refusing to add unnecessary automation.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="No single method carries the Lighthouse moonshot"}
**The system spans the stack.** Our mobile extended-reality (XR) target requires a complete hardware and software stack spanning all eight layers: workload traces (XRBench, SPEC2026, MLPerf), an ISA and ABI contract (RV64GCV), a precise compute organization (vector-capable CPU, accelerator, SoC block), careful memory and data movement choices (hierarchy, NoC bisection bandwidth, DRAM timing), strict adherence to a 3\ W TDP power envelope, a robust compiler and runtime stack (including Triton, an open-source GPU compiler language, LLVM, and MLIR), physical constraints (TSMC N7 and 3\ nm-class LP mobile process), and rigorous reliability and verification (SVA, UPF, STA signoff) across all resulting interfaces. We cannot rely on any single method to cover that entire chain.

**Assistance has several roles.** We can use a retrieval system to assemble our current workload, ISA, compiler, package, and tool constraints. We can deploy predictors to screen out microarchitecture and physical risks early on. An optimizer allows us to compare complex mappings and resource allocations, while generators can draft our RTL, compiler support, or tests. Finally, a tool-using system can automatically run our simulators and implementation checks, effortlessly routing failures back to the relevant stage for review.

**Shared assumptions remain mandatory.** The Lighthouse example also clearly shows the limits of this decomposition. Every component in our pipeline must refer to the same underlying workload, interfaces, and technology assumptions. Even with all this assistance, our selected design still needs executable software, stronger physical analysis, and independent verification. While assistance can connect and accelerate our work, it cannot turn an inconsistent set of local results into a sound, reliable system design.
:::

The public AlphaChip debate perfectly illustrates this same boundary. Producing a macro placement quickly is a completely different claim from establishing its routed physical quality. We have seen that comparisons of learned placement inherently depend on specific cases, compute budgets, implementation details, and downstream checks [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. While we won't resolve that technical disagreement here, its crucial lesson for our discussion is clear. Candidate-production speed can never stand in for matched, rigorous downstream evaluation.

Ultimately, no single AI method diagnoses its own need, performs the required work, and supplies an independent check all at the same time. As architects, we still completely own the question, the scope, the comparison, and the final decision.

\FloatBarrier

## Common Pitfalls

Deploying AI assistance inside the design loop frequently exposes anti-patterns where candidate generation velocity outpaces evaluation capacity. As system boundaries expand and multi-stage evaluation becomes expensive, design teams risk conflating local optimization speed with systemic progress. The following pitfalls detail how uncalibrated generation loops and compounding evaluation bottlenecks distort architectural decision-making.

**Conflating Candidate Generation Throughput with Evaluation Capacity.** Assuming that generating hundreds of candidate microarchitectures or floorplans per hour represents genuine progress. Generating options is cheap, but evaluating them accurately against cycle-accurate simulation, formal verification, and physical EDA signoff demands immense computational and human resources. Expanding generation velocity without scaling evaluation capacity creates severe queue backlogs and forces teams to drop essential validation checks.[^fn-homeostasis-c02]

[^fn-homeostasis-c02]: **Homeostatic system dynamics**: In general systems theory, open systems maintain dynamic equilibrium (homeostasis) through balanced throughput across stage boundaries. Unchecked candidate generation without proportional evaluation capacity disrupts system homeostasis, converting queued proposals into parasitic evaluation backlogs.

**Evaluating Hardware Candidates Without Co-Optimized Software.** Treating hardware block exploration as independent of the executing software stack. Specialized accelerators evaluated against unoptimized compiler flags, stale kernel libraries, or mismatched memory layouts yield misleading performance estimates. When candidate generation loops optimize hardware in isolation, selected configurations frequently stall in deployment under real software workloads.

**Ignoring Downstream Physical Design and Integration Bottlenecks.** Ranking candidate blocks purely on high-level analytical metrics or floorplan proxies while ignoring routing congestion, power delivery networks, and clock domain crossings. Fast candidate generators often select high-density layouts that fail physical synthesis or require prolonged wire-delay debug cycles, shifting engineering costs further downstream in the design loop.[^fn-horowitz-wire-scaling-c02]

[^fn-horowitz-wire-scaling-c02]: **Horowitz energy and wire scaling**: Interconnect wire energy and RC delay scale poorly relative to logic gates in deep submicron nodes [@Horowitz2014Energy; @HoMaiHorowitz2001FutureOfWires]. High-level floorplan generators that optimize logic density without extracting global routing delay and power delivery networks (PDN) frequently trigger severe timing and thermal signoff failures.

**Surrogate Model Exploitation and Uncalibrated Screening.** Relying on fast machine learning surrogate models to filter candidates without periodic re-calibration against high-fidelity EDA tools. Learned proxies exploit blind spots in their training distribution, nominating candidates that look optimal to the surrogate but fail gate-level timing or thermal limits during signoff.[^fn-goodharts-law-c02]

[^fn-goodharts-law-c02]: **Goodhart's Law and proxy gaming**: When an evaluation metric or proxy model becomes an explicit optimization target, it ceases to be a reliable measure. Learned ML surrogates exploit out-of-distribution inaccuracies, nominating candidate microarchitectures that optimize surrogate predictions while violating actual physical EDA timing constraints.

**Relocating Bottlenecks Downstream Instead of Eliminating Work.** Accelerating early RTL synthesis or candidate draft creation while leaving verification debug, coverage closure, and manual review unassisted. Shifting the system bottleneck downstream creates massive evaluation congestion, increasing total turn-around time even as generation metrics appear to improve.[^fn-amdahl-bottleneck-c02]

[^fn-amdahl-bottleneck-c02]: **Amdahl's Law of design throughput**: Accelerating a non-limiting phase of the design loop yields diminishing returns on overall time-to-tapeout [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. Accelerating RTL drafting while downstream formal verification and physical signoff remain manual simply shifts queue congestion downstream without reducing total turnaround time.

## Open Questions

What fundamental research questions define the boundary between automated design exploration and downstream evaluation capacity? As we transition from manual architectural exploration to AI-augmented generation, we face a critical frontier in figuring out how to balance candidate creation with rigorous evaluation. When we scale up our ability to propose new designs, navigating those choices against compounding physical, software, and integration constraints becomes profoundly difficult. The questions we outline below aren't just operational hurdles for our engineering teams, they represent foundational research problems worthy of doctoral dissertations or dedicated papers. Solving them is essential if we want to untangle exactly where our design loops are bottlenecked. We must ensure our new methodologies drive actual progress, rather than simply shoving an unsustainable evaluation burden further downstream.

**Diagnosing compounding pressure.** We only see the true value of AI assistance when it relieves the work that actually delays our architectural decisions, rather than just hiding or relocating the burden.

- **How can we reliably identify the true limiting constraint in an ongoing project?** Before deploying AI assistance, we need to know whether we're blocked on generating architectural candidates, running simulations, debugging SoC composition, or passing physical signoff. Our challenge lies in extracting this ground truth from tool logs, traces, and work records to ensure that any intervention will actually accelerate our final decision.

- **How can we detect when an intervention merely shifts a bottleneck downstream?** If we use generative models to rapidly propose specialized accelerator designs, we risk overwhelming our simulation, verification, and expert review capacity. We need reliable signals across our complete tool path to distinguish a genuine reduction in engineering effort from a costly queue shift.

**Managing evaluation capacity.** We can only benefit from a massive design space if we possess the simulation, physical verification, and review capacity to actually identify our best candidates.

- **How can we detect when candidate generation outpaces evaluation?** Because different candidates require vastly different levels of checking, from high-level performance proxies to cycle-accurate simulation, FPGA prototyping, and power delivery analysis, simple backlog growth can be dangerously misleading. Our core research problem is identifying when this capacity imbalance threatens our timeline and budget, well before it prevents a supported decision.

- **When does expanding the design space actively harm our final result?** Given our fixed evaluation and review budgets, generating more candidates can either uncover a breakthrough design or spread our verification efforts far too thin. The open problem is defining the precise threshold where adding more architectural choices dilutes our evidence, leaving our final decision weakly supported.

## Conclusion

How do we distill compounding design loop pressures into actionable principles for AI-assisted architecture?

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Relieve the True Limiting Constraint"}
System complexity shifts the bottlenecks of architectural design. To accelerate progress, explicitly identify whether exploration, evaluation, verification, or review limits the next architectural decision. Target automation or AI assistance strictly at this limiting work without relocating the burden downstream. Progress is valid only when the resulting comparison rigorously preserves workload definitions, executable software paths, physical constraints, evaluation costs, and authoritative verification.
:::


System complexity changes what a fair architecture comparison must carry.
Microarchitecture, specialization, system composition, evolving software,
physical constraints, evaluation cost, and verification add coupled work rather
than independent concerns. A local improvement can easily shift costs elsewhere in the
system or expose constraints that an earlier model omitted.

The technology dividend has also changed. More transistors no longer produce
proportional frequency or single-thread performance automatically. Architects
must obtain more of the benefit through parallelism, specialization, software,
and composition, while the cost of evaluating and verifying those choices
continues to rise. A large design space matters only when the team can evaluate
enough of it, at sufficient fidelity, to change the pending architecture
decision.

Those pressures make AI assistance worth investigating. Retrieval can assemble
scattered context, predictors can ration expensive evaluation, generators can
draft artifacts, optimizers can search large spaces, and tool-using systems can
connect proposals to existing engineering checks. None of these roles is
universally helpful, and none makes its own output trustworthy.

Ultimately, architects must evaluate the complete architecture work. A hardware
claim inherits its workload, software path, physical assumptions, tool state,
and verification. AI assistance earns its place when it improves that complete
comparison while preserving the measurements and checks that can reject a flawed
design. Applying it well therefore requires a systematic way to organize
AI-assisted design work, which @sec-architecture-20-ontology takes up.
